content:
Hi all,

I would like to start contributing a ClassicalFieldTheory development to PhysLib, based mainly on Chapter 5 of Cortés--Haupt, Mathematical Methods of Classical Physics.

My plan is to proceed in small PRs, starting with the local Lagrangian setup in Section 5.1:

  • fields and local jet data
  • local Lagrangians and action
  • total derivatives
  • Euler-Lagrange operators and equations
  • total divergences and equivalent Lagrangians

If this direction seems reasonable, I would later like to extend it toward the rest of Chapter 5:

  • automorphisms and conservation laws / Noether theorem
  • examples such as sigma models and Yang-Mills
  • energy-momentum tensor

Before going too far, I wanted to ask whether this overall organization and naming scheme seems appropriate for PhysLib, and whether there are conventions I should follow for structuring this area.

Thanks!

Hey @A98 (btw it's convention here to use real names as usernames),

I think this is a great idea! We already have (local) variational calculus in PhysLib, and this should ideally build of this.

We were recently talking about the geometric approach to the Harmonic oscillator. This is something I started in PhysLib#1004. Here you only need tangent bundles, but you may have ideas that can feed into that, or have suggestions for improvement for that PR. In any case, this may also be a good place to start to test your ideas. Likewise with other classical mechanics (rather than field theory) problems.

Thank you for planning small PRs - this really helps.

My big worry is that I don't think we have the definition of jet bundles in Mathlib, so if one wants to go above the first-level (i.e. just the tangent bundle), then you might need to get creative - though I guess this is why you are talking about local jet data.

wrt organising, I think you should really think here about building APIs - that is define what the key objects are (e.g. the lagrangian) and try and add all of the little lemmas and definitions that go around those key objects. This helps with organisation and maintainability.
(Should be relatively easy to define global variational calculus on a manifold from the local version.)

Hi Joseph,

thanks for your reply, it is very helpful. I took your comments on board:

  • building on the existing variational calculus in PhysLib,
  • thinking in terms of API design around the key objects,
  • and starting locally rather than trying to force global jet-bundle machinery too early.

With that in mind, I have been sketching a first roadmap. My current idea is to start with a local development aimed at Theorem 5.2 in Cortés--Haupt, i.e. the local Euler–Lagrange equations for a k-th order Lagrangian on an open set Ω ⊆ ℝ^n under compactly supported variations.

More concretely, I am currently thinking of proceeding in small PRs along the following lines:

  • multi-indices and iterated partial derivatives,
  • local jet data (rather than global jet bundles),
  • total derivative operators,
  • local Lagrangians and the action functional,
  • the local Euler–Lagrange operator and the first variation formula,
  • then the theorem identifying critical points of the action with solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equations.

So the idea would be to keep the first stage entirely local and API-focused, and only later think about how to package this more geometrically / globally.

At the moment I am tentatively thinking this should live somewhere like
PhysLean/ClassicalFieldTheory/Local/...
unless there is a better place that would fit more naturally

Thanks!

P.S: Here it is my name! :P

Sounds good to me! Multi-indices and iterated partial derivatives should likely go directly in e.g. Space.Derivatives...... Otherwise PhysLean/ClassicalFieldTheory/Local/... seems a good.

(Also I don't want to dissuade you from doing global jet bundles, I just think it might be difficult :), though jet bundles can be defined from a local setting anyway, so maybe we don't lose anything here).

Thanks for updating your user name :).

I now have a local formalization of the core of Theorem 5.2 from Cortés--Haupt on a branch.

The development stays entirely local, following the plan we discussed earlier: multi-indices and iterated derivatives, admissible compactly supported variations, local jet data, total derivatives, local Lagrangians and the action functional, the local Euler--Lagrange operator, and finally the first-variation criterion. The Euler--Lagrange criterion is derived under explicit smoothness/admissibility hypotheses suited to the current local setup.

At the current local stage, the final criterion is formulated under the following explicit hypotheses:

  • the field f is smooth;
  • the local Lagrangian L is smooth in explicit local jet coordinates;
  • the pair (L, f) is admissible for the action, i.e. the action density is integrable;
  • variations are admissible and compactly supported.

Following your earlier remarks, the reusable pieces are kept outside the field-theory namespace where appropriate: multi-indices live in reusable data-structure infrastructure, iterated derivatives and bounded derivative indices live in Space.Derivatives, and the field-theory-specific local API currently lives in PhyslibAlpha/ClassicalFieldTheory/Local/....

The original core-Physlib stack was reorganized during review. PRs 1--5 introduced the reusable foundations directly in core Physlib, and the local CFT stack itself was then moved to PhyslibAlpha so that it can be developed and reviewed more quickly before deciding which mature pieces should move back to core.

Current status:

  • PR 1: MultiIndex — merged
  • PR 2: Iterated derivatives I — merged
  • PR 3: Iterated derivatives II — merged
  • PR 4: Admissible variations — merged
  • PR 5: DerivativeIndex — merged
  • Alpha PR: local CFT first-variation stack — merged

The merged Alpha stack contains the coordinate-level local CFT pipeline: jet points, coordinate jet fiber directions, jet regularity/support, total derivatives, local Lagrangians, local action and criticality, the Euler--Lagrange operator, and the first-variation criterion.

The next small Alpha PRs I am planning are:

  • first-order specialization for k = 1;
  • total divergences and equivalent Lagrangians;
  • small examples / bridge to existing mechanics code;
  • later, possible migration of mature reusable pieces from Alpha back into core Physlib.

I will keep using this thread to track the current direction as the Alpha stack evolves.
